newsitem.title: HUNGARY: New scandal revelations could damage Horn-analysts.
newsitem.headline: New scandal revelations could damage Horn-analysts.

text.p: New evidence implicating Prime Minister Gyula Horn's Socialist Party in a 1996 privatisation scandal could seriously undermine Horn's position within the government, analysts said on Wednesday.
"New evidence could bring into question Horn's integrity," political analyst Tibor Vidos told Reuters.

A Budapest court started proceedings on Wednesday in the so-called "Tocsik affair", in which an adviser to the APV state privatisation agency Marta Tocsik received $5 million for negotiating land deals with municipalities on APV's behalf.
The court will examine the validity of contracts signed by APV in the affair, a process which is expected to last several months.
Revelations of the payments led Horn to dismiss last October the entire APV board and the minister in charge of privatisation, Tamas Suchman.
On Monday Hungary's Chief Prosecutor Kalman Gyorgyi asked parliament to lift Socialist Party treasurer Laszlo Boldvai's parliamentary immunity following evidence that may implicate him in the affair.
The move follows repeated denials by Horn that his party was involved in the scandal.
"Boldvai is a prominent Socialist party figure, so it is now a question of party officials being involved," another analyst Attila Ledenyi told Reuters.
The Socialists' junior coalition partner, the Free Democrats (SZDSZ), have also been implicated through Gyorgy Budai, a businessman with close SZDSZ ties, whom Gyorgyi also cited.

Gyorgyi's letter to parliament said Boldvai and Budai told Tocsik she could keep her success fee if she transferred 25 percent of one instalment of the fee into accounts named by the two men, which she did.
Analysts said the Socialist Party's possible involvement in the Tocsik case could prompt the opposition to ask for Horn's resignation.
"All the more so, because SZDSZ President Ivan Peto offered his resignation earlier when a low-rank member of his party was named in the affair," Ledenyi said.

Vidos, however, thinks the ruling coalition's comfortable majority minimises the danger of Horn resigning but the scandal could play into the hands of those in his party who are seeking to replace him.
"The party could come to the conclusion that in the 1998 (general) elections Horn would be a liability rather than an asset," Vidos said.
